front.title: Autonomous Machine Payments: Persistent Financial State Channels for Machine-to-Machine Transactions

abstract.t: This document defines the Autonomous Machine Payments (AMP) protocol, a mechanism for persistent financial state channels between autonomous agents and services. AMP replaces per-request payment models with persistent channels that allow unlimited interactions after a single channel-opening transaction, with periodic net settlement. The protocol is designed for machine-to-machine payment flows where agents operate autonomously with budgets, ongoing relationships, and multi-step workflows. AMP defines the channel lifecycle (discovery, open, consume, settle, close), metering modes, delegation semantics, and transport bindings for HTTP, WebSocket, gRPC, MQTT, MCP (JSON-RPC), and raw TCP.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: HTTP 402 "Payment Required" was reserved in HTTP/1.1 but has seen limited standardized use. Recent protocols such as the Payment HTTP Authentication Scheme have begun to define semantics for 402-based payment flows between machines.

Existing payment protocols treat each API request as a discrete payment event. This creates per-call latency (additional round-trips for payment negotiation), per-call on-chain transaction costs, and stateless interactions where each request is financially independent. Autonomous agents do not operate this way: they maintain ongoing relationships with services, execute against budgets, open streaming connections, and delegate sub-tasks to other agents.

The Autonomous Machine Payments (AMP) protocol addresses this by introducing persistent financial state channels. A funder opens a channel once, depositing funds into a program-controlled escrow account. Subsequent requests are served without per-request payment negotiation. Usage is metered off-chain by the service and settled periodically via net clearing. This reduces on-chain transactions from N (one per request) to approximately 3 (open, settle, close) regardless of request volume.

section.name: Design Principles
section.t: AMP is designed around four principles:

ol.li: Zero runtime friction: after channel open, consumption adds zero payment latency to the request path.
Transport agnostic: the protocol works on HTTP, WebSocket, gRPC, MQTT, MCP (JSON-RPC), and raw TCP.
Ledger native: channel state is stored on-chain as a program-derived account, composable with other on-chain programs.
Credit-ready: the channel model is architecturally compatible with credit and reputation extensions that allow channels to operate with reduced or zero deposits.

section.name: Relationship to Other Specifications
section.t: AMP uses HTTP 402 for initial pricing discovery, consistent with . However, after discovery, AMP's channel lifecycle diverges: instead of per-request challenge-credential flows, AMP establishes a persistent channel that serves unlimited requests without additional payment negotiation per call.
AMP is complementary to payment-method-agnostic frameworks. It defines a specific channel-based payment mechanism optimized for high-frequency machine-to-machine interactions with net settlement.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dl.dd: A persistent financial state object between two parties (funder and recipient), represented as an on-chain account. A channel holds deposited tokens in a vault and tracks usage state. Lifecycle: Open, Active, Settled (repeating), Closed.
The party that deposits funds into a channel. Typically an autonomous agent or client application.
The party that receives funds via settlement. Typically a service provider operating an API.
Off-chain usage tracking performed by the recipient. The recipient tracks how much the funder has consumed and produces signed metering proofs that authorize on-chain settlement.
The process of transferring owed funds from the channel vault to the recipient. Settlement is always net: one on-chain transaction covers all usage since the last settlement.
Assignment of consumption rights from a funder to a third-party public key (the delegate). The delegate can consume services against the channel up to a specified limit.
The process by which a recipient of an upstream channel creates a downstream channel funded from the upstream vault. This enables agent supply chains where value flows through a chain of services.

A signed attestation by the recipient of the total usage during a settlement period. Contains the amount owed, call count, period timestamps, sequence number range, and the recipient's Ed25519 signature over a hash of these fields.

section.name: Protocol Overview
section.t: AMP defines a channel-based payment protocol with five phases: discovery, open, consume, settle, and close. The following diagram illustrates the message flow:

figure.name: AMP Protocol Flow
figure.artwork: Client Server | | | (1) GET /.well-known/amp.json | |----------------------------------------------->| | (2) 200 OK { pricing manifest } | |<-----------------------------------------------| | | | (3) Open channel on ledger | | (single on-chain transaction) | | | | (4) GET /resource | | AMP-Channel: <channel-id> | | AMP-Seq: 1 | | AMP-Sig: <signature> | |----------------------------------------------->| | (5) 200 OK { resource } | | AMP-Balance: <remaining> | |<-----------------------------------------------| | | | ... repeat (4)-(5) unlimited times ... | | ... zero on-chain transactions ... | | | | (6) Server settles periodically | | (single on-chain transaction, | | nets all accumulated usage) | | | | (7) Close channel | | (final settlement + refund remainder) | | |

section.t: Steps (4) and (5) repeat for every API call. No on-chain transactions occur during consumption. The server meters usage off-chain and settles periodically (step 6) via a single on-chain transaction that covers all usage since the last settlement.
For 1,000 API calls, a per-request protocol requires 1,000 on-chain transactions. AMP requires approximately 3 (open, settle, close), regardless of call volume.

section.name: Discovery
section.t: Before opening a channel, the client MUST discover the server's AMP pricing. Three discovery mechanisms are defined.

section.name: Well-Known Endpoint
section.t:
The server SHOULD expose pricing at the well-known URI
"/.well-known/amp.json". The response is a JSON object with the following fields:
The "pricing" object MUST contain a "default" field with the following sub-fields:

tr.td: Cost per unit in token smallest unit

section.t: The "pricing" object MAY contain a "routes" field: a JSON object where keys are route path prefixes and values are partial pricing configurations that override the default.

section.name: HTTP 402 Response Headers
section.t: On any request to an AMP-enabled endpoint without valid channel credentials, the server MUST respond with HTTP 402 Payment Required and include the following response header fields:
The response body SHOULD contain a JSON error object with "error", "message", and "amp_version" fields.

section.name: In-Band Signaling
section.t: For non-HTTP transports (WebSocket, gRPC, MQTT, raw TCP), the server MUST send AMP pricing as the first message or frame after connection establishment, using the same JSON schema as the well-known endpoint.

section.name: Open
section.t: The client creates a channel by submitting an "open_channel" instruction to the on-chain AMP program.

ol.li: The client derives the channel account address using deterministic address derivation with seeds: ["amp-channel", funder_pubkey, recipient_pubkey, nonce] where nonce is encoded as a little-endian unsigned 64-bit integer (8 bytes). The client SHOULD use nonce 0 for the first channel with a given recipient.
The client submits the open instruction with: recipient, token mint, deposit amount, rate limit, settlement interval, and nonce.
On confirmation, funds transfer from the client's token account to a program-controlled vault account.
The client sends the channel address to the server via the appropriate transport binding (e.g., AMP-Channel header for HTTP).

section.t: The server MUST verify the channel on-chain before accepting requests: the account exists, is owned by the AMP program, the recipient field matches the server's public key, the status is Active (0), the balance is greater than zero, and the token mint is accepted.

section.name: Consume
section.t: After channel open, the client includes channel credentials with every request. For HTTP, three header fields are used:

tr.td: Ed25519 signature of the sequence number (base58-encoded)

section.t: The AMP-Sig value is an Ed25519 signature computed over the sequence number encoded as a little-endian unsigned 64-bit integer (8 bytes), using the funder's keypair (or the delegate's keypair if delegation is active).
The server MUST perform all of the following verification steps:

ol.li: Verify the channel account exists on-chain and has status Active. The server MAY cache channel state with a TTL.
Verify the signature matches the channel's funder public key or delegate public key.
Verify the sequence number is strictly greater than the last seen sequence number for this channel.
Verify the channel balance is greater than zero.
Serve the request.
Increment the local metering counter for this channel.

section.t: Zero on-chain transactions occur during consumption. All verification is performed off-chain using cached channel state and Ed25519 signature verification.
The server SHOULD include an AMP-Balance response header field containing the remaining channel balance as an integer in the token's smallest unit.

section.name: Settle
section.t: Settlement is triggered when any of the following conditions are met:

ul.li: The settle_interval seconds have elapsed since the last settlement timestamp.
Accumulated usage exceeds a server-defined threshold.

section.t: The settlement process is:

ol.li: The server constructs a Metering Proof (see ).
The server submits the "settle" instruction to the AMP program with the settlement amount.
The program verifies: the amount does not exceed the balance, the settle_interval has elapsed, and the settler is either the recipient or the authorized netting authority (if configured).

On success, the program transfers the amount from the vault to the recipient's token account and updates the channel state: balance decreases, total consumed increases, and the last settlement timestamp is set to the current time.

section.name: Top-Up
section.t: The funder MAY add funds to an active channel at any time by submitting the "top_up" instruction with the desired amount. The channel balance and total deposited values increase accordingly. Top-up does not affect metering, settlement timing, or sequence numbers.

section.name: Close
section.t: Either party MAY close a channel by submitting the "close_channel" instruction.

ol.li: An optional final settlement amount is transferred to the recipient.
The remaining balance is returned to the funder's token account.
The channel and vault accounts are closed, and rent-exempt reserves are returned to the funder.

section.t: A channel with active downstream channels (from channel chaining) MUST NOT be closed until all downstream channels are closed first.
After closure, the server MUST reject any subsequent requests referencing this channel with error code AMP_CLOSED.

section.name: Metering
section.t: Metering is off-chain usage tracking performed by the server. All metering happens off-chain; no on-chain transaction occurs during consumption. The following metering modes are defined:

tr.td: Server publishes a custom metering function

section.name: Metering Proof Signature Scheme
section.t: The server signs the following data to produce a metering proof:
The signed payload is the concatenation of 7 fields, totaling 80 bytes:

ul.li: channel_id: 32 bytes (raw public key of the channel account)
period_start: 8 bytes (little-endian signed 64-bit integer, Unix timestamp)
period_end: 8 bytes (little-endian signed 64-bit integer, Unix timestamp)

section.t: The hash is SHA-256 of the 80-byte payload, producing a 32-byte digest. The signature is Ed25519 over the 32-byte digest using the recipient's keypair.

section.name: Channel State
section.t: The channel state is an on-chain account derived via deterministic address derivation from the seeds: ["amp-channel", funder_pubkey, recipient_pubkey, nonce]. The nonce is encoded as a little-endian unsigned 64-bit integer.
The vault is a separate token account controlled by the channel account, derived from: ["amp-vault", channel_account_address].
The channel state account contains the following fields (329 bytes of data after the 8-byte account discriminator):

section.name: Delegation
section.t: A funder MAY assign a delegate public key to their channel. The delegate can consume services against the channel up to a specified limit.
Only the funder MAY set or change the delegate. The delegate limit MUST NOT exceed the current channel balance. Setting a new delegate resets the delegate_consumed counter to zero.

During consumption, the server MUST accept signatures from either the funder's or the delegate's keypair. When the signer is the delegate, the server MUST track delegate consumption separately and reject requests that would exceed the delegate limit.

Delegation enables agent-to-agent budget forwarding: Agent A opens a channel, delegates a portion to Agent B, and Agent B consumes services against Agent A's channel without requiring its own capital.

section.name: Transport Bindings
section.t: AMP is transport agnostic. This section defines how AMP metadata is carried on each supported transport.

section.name: HTTP
section.t: Discovery uses the well-known endpoint () or 402 response headers (). Request credentials are carried as HTTP header fields: AMP-Channel, AMP-Seq, AMP-Sig. The server responds with AMP-Balance.

section.name: WebSocket
section.t: Discovery: the server sends pricing as the first text frame after the WebSocket handshake, using the same JSON schema as the well-known endpoint.
Channel binding: the client sends the first text frame as a JSON object with "amp_channel", "amp_seq", and "amp_sig" fields. The server acknowledges with "amp_status" and "amp_balance".

Subsequent messages use one of two formats: text mode (JSON wrapper with "amp_seq", "amp_sig", and "payload" fields) or binary mode (2-byte little-endian u16 sequence, 64-byte raw Ed25519 signature, followed by the application payload).

section.name: gRPC
section.t: AMP credentials are carried as gRPC metadata keys: "amp-channel", "amp-seq", "amp-sig". For streaming RPCs, credentials are sent in the initial request metadata; the server meters each response message.

section.name: MQTT 5.0
section.t: Discovery: the server publishes pricing to topic "$amp/pricing". Channel binding: the client includes AMP credentials as MQTT 5.0 CONNECT packet User Properties. Per-message metering: "amp-seq" and "amp-sig" as User Properties on each PUBLISH packet.

section.name: MCP (JSON-RPC 2.0)
section.t: An AMP-enabled MCP server MUST advertise pricing via a dedicated "amp/pricing" JSON-RPC method. The response includes per-tool pricing in a "tools" object within the pricing manifest.

When calling a paid tool, the client MUST include AMP credentials in the "_amp" field of the JSON-RPC "params" object, containing "channel", "seq", and "sig" fields. The "_amp" prefix is a reserved namespace; servers that do not support AMP MUST ignore fields prefixed with "_".

If credentials are missing, the server responds with JSON-RPC error code -32602 (Invalid Params), with the message set to the appropriate AMP error code and the "data" field containing pricing information.

section.name: Raw TCP
section.t: Discovery: the server sends pricing as the first frame. Frame format: 2-byte little-endian u16 envelope length, followed by a CBOR-encoded object with short keys ("c" for channel bytes, "s" for sequence number, "g" for signature bytes), followed by the application payload.

section.name: Error Codes
section.t: The following error codes are defined by AMP. Servers MUST use these codes in error responses across all transports.

tr.td: No valid channel for this request

section.t: Error responses for HTTP SHOULD use the following JSON format:
For non-HTTP transports, the same JSON schema is used as the error message payload.

section.name: Transport Security
section.t: All AMP communications SHOULD use TLS 1.3 or later. Channel credentials (AMP-Sig) authenticate individual requests but do not encrypt them. TLS provides confidentiality and integrity for the transport layer.

section.name: Replay Prevention
section.t: The client MUST include a monotonically increasing sequence number (AMP-Seq) with every request. The server MUST reject any request where the sequence number is less than or equal to the last seen sequence number for the given channel, and MUST respond with AMP_INVALID_SEQ.
The server SHOULD persist the last seen sequence number to survive process restarts.

section.name: Fund Custody
section.t: Channel funds are held in a program-controlled vault account. Neither the funder nor the recipient can directly access the vault. Funds can only move via the settle instruction (to the recipient, requiring a valid metering proof) or the close instruction (remainder to funder, settled amount to recipient).

section.name: Dispute Model
section.t: AMP uses a simple dispute model based on unilateral channel closure. If the server overcharges, the client can close the channel immediately. The client loses at most one unsettled period's worth of consumption. Shorter settle_interval values reduce the maximum loss in a dispute.

AMP does not implement on-chain dispute resolution. The trust assumption is that the server and client have aligned economic incentives and that the maximum loss per dispute is bounded and known in advance.

section.name: Rate Limiting
section.t: The rate_limit field constrains the maximum tokens that can be settled per settle_interval. This is enforced both on-chain (by the settle instruction) and off-chain (by the server middleware rejecting requests that would exceed the limit before the next settlement).

section.name: Sybil Resistance
section.t: Opening a channel requires an on-chain transaction (paying transaction fees), a token deposit (enforced by the server's minimum deposit), and rent-exempt balance for the channel and vault accounts. These costs make sybil channel attacks economically impractical.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Channel state is stored on-chain and is publicly readable. The funder's public key, recipient's public key, balance, and settlement history are visible to any observer. Parties requiring privacy should consider this when choosing deposit amounts and settlement intervals.

section.name: A.1. Basic Channel Lifecycle
section.t: Client discovers pricing:
Client opens channel (one on-chain transaction), then makes a paid request:
Subsequent requests increment AMP-Seq. Zero on-chain transactions occur. The server settles periodically. The client closes the channel when done.

section.name: A.2. Delegation Flow
section.t: Agent A opens a channel with a $10 deposit. Agent A sets a delegate (Agent B) with a $3 limit via the on-chain delegate instruction. Agent B signs requests using its own keypair, referencing Agent A's channel. The server verifies Agent B's signature against the delegate field in the on-chain channel state.

section.name: A.3. Channel Chaining
section.t: Agent A opens a channel with Service B ($10 deposit). Service B needs GPU compute from Service C, so it creates a downstream channel funded from Agent A's upstream vault ($3). The upstream balance decreases to $7. Service C settles the downstream channel. When the downstream channel closes, the remainder returns to Service B. When the upstream channel closes, the remainder returns to Agent A.
